title: Why Amazon Will Never Buy FedEx - Barron's
text:

https://www.barrons.com/articles/why-amazon-will-never-buy-fedex-51549015201 Why Amazon Will Never Buy FedEx By Feb. 1, 2019 5:00 a.m. ET Order Reprints Photograph by Spencer Platt/Getty Images Text size
Amazon.com (AMZN) should buy FedEx (FDX) because its stock is cheap . It’s an provocative idea, and cross-industry mergers are interesting to think about.
Loop Capital analyst Anthony Chukumba made the case this past week, and we wrote about it in Barron’s .
The reasoning used to justify such mergers can be difficult to refute. After all, you can’t argue with certainty that a deal could never happen. Still, Barron’s is comfortable saying an Amazon-FedEx tie-up is very, very unlikely.
There are two sets of issues that should scuttle this proposed deal: market issues and business issues. Let’s tackle the former first.
Read more: Antitrust and How the American Dream Is Becoming a Sucker’s Game
Chukumba covers tech stocks, and his Amazon price target is $2,200 a share. That is equal to 61 times Amazon’s estimated 2019 earnings. It’s no wonder he thinks FedEx is cheap at 10.7 times estimated earnings. Chukumba is used to analyzing and valuing high-multiple stocks with powerful secular trends—like online shopping—that support high growth rates. FedEx is a completely different, economically sensitive company.
This kind of confusion arises when growth investors wander off “Growth Island” and swim onto “Value Investing Island.” The two groups aren’t always accepting of outsiders. They try to communicate, but they speak very different valuation languages.
Consider Tesla (TSLA). Baird analyst Ben Kallo rates Tesla shares Outperform, with a $465 target price. That’s 50% higher than Tesla’s current share price. Kallo doesn’t cover cars, he covers energy and sustainable technologies like solar power and waste-grease recycling.
Most of the Sell ratings on Tesla shares actually come from traditional automotive analysts who struggle to justify Tesla’s share price when General Motors (GM) trades for six times estimated 2019 earnings. Tesla shares trade for 57 times estimated 2019 earnings.
Of course, a pair of fresh eyes can help reframe an investment and uncover hidden value. But it’s unlikely.
The business-related problems with the proposal are even more daunting.
Amazon, which is interested in getting products to customers in two days or less, doesn’t really need FedEx’s massive infrastructure—and e-commerce is only a small portion of FedEx’s business. “FedEx’s upstream sorting capability is fundamentally different than last-mile delivery capacity,” explains Baird transportation analyst Ben Hartford.
There are other reasons a deal is inlikely, according to Cowen transportation analyst Helane Becker. FedEx competitor United Parcel Service (UPS) would try to stop the deal in court. And FedEx founder and CEO Fred Smith, the largest single FedEx shareholder of [FedEx], would have to agree to a deal—a dim possibility, she points out.
Finally, there are antitrust issues—and they have nothing to do with President Donald Trump lashing out against Amazon in the past via tweets.
Vertical mergers are facing more regulatory scrutiny. Those are deals when a company expands up or down its value chain. Horizontal deals, by contrast, are the ones when a company buys another in its industry. Horizontal mergers are the ones that have historically faced higher scrutiny because of fears that a company is amassing too much market power.
The Justice Department, for example, tried to stop American Airlines Group (AAL) from buying US Air, fearing that a more concentrated airline industry would mean higher prices for traveling consumers. That deal eventually went through.
In 2017, the Justice Department filed a complaint challenging AT&T ’s (T) proposed acquisition of Time Warner in November of that year, though the deal ultimately went through. Any vertical deal involving Amazon could generate even more scrutiny than the AT&T media deal.
What Amazon really wants is to supplement its logistic capabilities, like Walmart (WMT) did when the chain was growing rapidly. Walmart is one of the largest tractor-trailer operators in the U.S., but it never bought a public trucking company, and the trucking industry survived.
Amazon told Barron’s it uses a variety of carriers but had no information about potential deals. UPS said it doesn’t comment on speculation and FedEx wasn’t immediately available for comment.
Even if a deal won’t happen, it’s still fun to think out of the box. And sometimes the mental gymnastics can yield a moneymaking idea.
Richard Parsons thought phone companies were an existential threat to cable over a decade ago. Now AT&T owns Time Warner. The convergence of entertainment delivery and content production is a fait accompli. Even Barron’s thinks that Apple (AAPL) should buy Nintendo (7974. Japan) to gain access to gaming content that could reduce Apple’s reliance on hardware sales.
